This is cope. People from prestigious schools have a network of connections built-in to their school that can get them work based solely on that. Their "intelligence" in abstract is more or less irrelevant.
 The only thing that really matters to employers is perceived competence, and people from prestigious schools who can get opportunities from people they know have a lot of perceived competence. Actual competence is difficult to determine for people without long and well documented work histories relevant to the particular role, so it's just simply not an important factor.

The uncomfortable truth here is Big Tech and F500 companies are filled with unpleasant people that break all these rules OP listed because they simply get things done (whether they are actually good at their job is debatable, what matters is many of them put on a good show for leadership and play the corporate game well).
 And guess what, unpleasant people who are in the position of hiring often hire (or even select for) other unpleasant people.
 This is all to say, many new grads/early career folks will pretty quickly learn being a normal person is unfortunately not selected for at a lot of tech companies and very few interviewers can even glean that info from a ~1hr interview.

Totally agree. I don’t go to a T20 School, I don’t consider myself a ‘cracked’ student, but I put in the work on practicing my LeetCode, SQL, and Behavioral Prep, played the game of talking to professionals and getting referrals, and have a well-paying offer for the upcoming summer already.
 The game’s not impossible, the problem is either that a person isn’t reading the rules and aimlessly wandering through university, or the opposite problem of a person spending too much time focusing on strategy and forgetting to put in the boring labor.

This frankly sounds like a mental health issue not a CS issue. The competitive jobs are often about passing screening tests and having good references, soft and interpersonal skills. My kid recently graduated from a regular public university in flyover country and landed a competitive 6 figure job working with elite grads. 
 Lots of people burn put on the super intense jobs. Google is an especially bad employer. My spouse and I both have CS degrees and have worked and hired in tech. Is he working at all? I’d suspect depression and/or anxiety. I think young people can get fixated on dream schools and dream jobs and they should think bigger about a dream life with some balance. The average first tech job lasts like a couple years. And you learn and move on. And you might do that a few times before settling in or changing course.

I think this is where I "got lucky" with my first entry-level job. Wasn't at a career fair, but among the dozens of companies I applied to was a small company most people haven't heard of. They didn't have someone whose entire job was recruiting, it was two senior engineers/managers from the office trying to hire new engineers in addition to their more-than-full-time technical work. They responded promptly to emails and felt a lot more genuine than larger companies' recruiters. I don't think they were just hiring anyone they could get (interview was pretty extensive with multiple programming tests) but I'm guessing they didn't get a ton of interest considering the lack of name recognition.
 I got the offer letter probably within a week of interviewing. Meanwhile, L3Harris took like 6 months to send me their stock rejection email after I had already accepted the job and made moving arrangements 🤣
 tldr yes go talk to small companies. Especially in cybersecurity/hardware engineering/defense, those seem to have decent job security compared to other cs jobs.

Like, that company is worth 100m right now, and if you think in 2-3 years it'll be worth a billion, then that equity is worth 1-5 million USD. And miners work very long and hard hours too, for much less pay than 300-500k a year. (Good pay, but not that much.)
 Obviously it's a crazy company, but then again all startups that look to be moonshots are, and that's how the original people there ended up being worth a lot. Do you think Anthropic or OpenAI's early employees, who are worth tens or hundreds of millions, get there by working a 40-hour-a-week job? No shade if it's not for you; most people have more important things in their 20s and 30s than working 80h weeks, like having friends or family, enjoying nature or pets. But why are you looking at jobs offering 80h weeks if that's not your preference, and then complaining about them not being your fit?

 He's preemptively getting disappointed as he realizes joining the top 1% of tech firms isn't realistic for the majority of graduates. Not anymore than every basketball enthusiast will be in the NBA.
 I'm saying that is a tiny portion of companies hiring and he's setting his sights too narrow to see the tens of thousands of trash SMBs who have tons of tech debt and need problem solvers.
 They're not jobs that will have your friends and family bragging about "my so and so who works at Google," or give you an inflated personal image, but they will pay the bills.

While it is true that the job market was better a decade ago, the aesthetic being sold here is a fabricaution.
 Yes, you were paid well. Yes, you were given goody bags and got to go into a high rise glass monolith. 
 But no, you were never an erudite, sweater-wearing, genius happily coding away on a beanbag share surrounded by lattes and attractive people. You were an overworked instrument of a corporation leveraged for a profit that could be dug out of your skull through your fingers by means of typing computer code. And, when the bill came due, that instrument was excised with as much thought as eliminating a malignant growth.
 As the saying goes: the chains are golden handcuffs, but chains nonetheless.

I can agree, most group projects I had bar literally the few I had with a good student/friend were very lack luster and often people wouldn’t even take time to read the “Quick Start” guides for language/tool/etc. 
Our capstone was an automated DMV scheduling system with what was supposed to be a static HTML UI. Ended up being sloppified React because of inserting random or duplicate JS/CSS/HTML into every page was more annoying than using React for a project that DID NOT NEED React but at least everyone’s prompts didn’t break the codebase. 
On top of that it was Agile Sprint based so you had this lack of knowledge (me included used to GH Kanban/Issues) on when to close task, what review means when the review process is “that looks good”/random test’s passing, etc. I don’t even wanna type about the Python FastAPI/SQLAlchemy backend 
(I wanted to use Go but no one knew it so Python it is)
Also Git for most of my team was a an annoying tool to push code to a website not version control so be warned 😂
Basically try your best and have fun with what you can do I enjoyed every project for the most part. But, do not count on your team to be as enthusiastic as you might be.
